userJob: Make the typographic argument survive the moment before the webfont arrives, and the machine where it never does
problem: A face is chosen and the fallback stack is whatever was in the boilerplate. On a slow connection the page is read in the fallback for a second; on a machine without the face it is read in the fallback forever, and the whole argument is carried by a font that may not be there.
worksWhen: Always, and most sharply when the faces are system faces rather than webfonts
mechanism: Write the fallback stack out, in order, ending in a generic family. Say whether the first fallback is metrically compatible: if it is not, swap reflows the page when the real face lands, and that is a decision rather than an accident. Then render the page with the face blocked and look at it.
risks: A stack ending in a named font, so a machine with none of them falls back to the browser default and the line lengths change
Choosing optional to avoid the reflow, which means many readers never see the chosen face at all
mobileRules: Test the fallback at 375 first: a wider fallback is where the overflow appears, and it appears at the narrowest width.
accessibilityRules: A face swap that moves content under a reader’s finger or cursor is a failure whatever it looks like
Never block rendering on a font. Text that is not there is worse than text in the wrong face.
genericnessNote: The generic fallbacks are the same for everyone, which is what makes them fallbacks. The risk is that a page with no webfont IS its fallback stack, and Georgia plus Segoe UI is the most ordinary pair on the internet.

userJob: Choose faces that can actually set the words this page contains
problem: A face is chosen from an English specimen and the page is Danish, Polish, Turkish or Vietnamese. The accented characters fall back silently to a different face, mid-word, and the line looks slightly wrong in a way nobody can name.
worksWhen: The page is in any language, which is all of them
mechanism: Name the scripts and the language coverage the page needs in the contract, then set the page’s hardest real string in every face and every fallback and look at it. Include the number formats: a Danish thousands separator is a full stop, and 2.200 must not read as two point two.
risks: Checking the display face and not the fallback, so the coverage gap only appears on machines without the face
Assuming a variable font carries every axis in every subset it ships
mobileRules: Subsetting for weight is fine; subsetting away the page’s own alphabet is the failure this prevents.
accessibilityRules: A word set half in one face and half in another is harder to read, and often fails at 200 per cent zoom before it fails at 100
genericnessNote: A coverage requirement narrows the field rather than shaping it.
